questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 2 mm² carries a current of 3.2 A. The number density of free electrons in copper is 5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The drift speed of the electrons is:

solution.concept: Current in terms of drift velocity: I = n e A v_d
solution.explanation: The current is carried by n electrons per unit volume, each of charge e, drifting with speed v_d through area A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m/s converts 2 mm² as 2 × 10⁻³ m². 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s uses A = 1 mm². 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s has an extra factor of 2 in the denominator.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance of the arrangement is:

solution.concept: Series and parallel combination of resistors
solution.explanation: Reduce the parallel pair first, then add the series resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 Ω puts all three in series. 4/3 Ω puts all three in parallel. 4.5 Ω inverts the parallel formula, taking (3 + 6)/(3 × 6) = 0.5 Ω.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected across an external resistance of 5.5 Ω. The potential difference across the terminals of the cell is:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage of a cell delivering current: V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: Part of the emf is used to drive the current through the cell's own internal resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 V is the emf, the terminal voltage only on open circuit. 1 V is the drop inside the cell (Ir). 13 V is ε + Ir, which applies only while the cell is being charged.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Kirchhoff's junction rule (the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it) is a consequence of the conservation of:

solution.concept: Basis of Kirchhoff's rules
solution.explanation: In steady state no charge piles up at a junction, so whatever charge flows in per second must flow out. The loop rule, in contrast, follows from the fact that the electrostatic force is conservative (energy).
steps: Junction rule: ΣI_in = ΣI_out → no accumulation of charge → conservation of charge
Loop rule: Σ(changes in potential) = 0 around a closed loop → conservation of energy
solution.why_others_wrong: Energy is the basis of the loop rule, not the junction rule. Momentum and angular momentum play no role in either rule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal wire has a resistance of 10 Ω at 20 °C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the metal is 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ (take it as constant, referred to 20 °C). Its resistance at 70 °C is:

solution.concept: Temperature dependence of resistance: R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]
solution.explanation: For a metal the resistance rises almost linearly with temperature over a moderate range.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.8 Ω uses ΔT = 70 °C instead of 50 °C. 8 Ω subtracts the change, as if α were negative. 10.2 Ω adds αΔT = 0.2 directly in ohms instead of multiplying it by R₀.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 5 Ω is drawn out (without any change in volume or resistivity) until its radius is half of its original value. The new resistance of the wire is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with constant volume
solution.explanation: When the radius halves, the area falls to one-fourth. Since the volume A·l is fixed, the length becomes four times. Both changes increase the resistance.
solution.shortcut: At constant volume, R ∝ 1/r⁴. Halving r multiplies R by 2⁴ = 16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 Ω counts only one of the two effects (length or area). 320 Ω takes the area factor as 16 instead of 4. 1.25 Ω divides by 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge, an unknown resistance X is in the left gap and a 12 Ω resistance is in the right gap. The null point is found at 40.0 cm from the left end of the wire. The value of X is:

solution.concept: Balance condition of a metre bridge: X/R = l/(100 − l)
solution.explanation: The metre bridge is a Wheatstone bridge whose two ratio arms are the two segments of a uniform wire, so their resistances are proportional to their lengths.
steps: Left segment l = 40 cm (on the side of X), right segment = 60 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 Ω inverts the ratio of the lengths. 4.8 Ω and 7.2 Ω multiply 12 Ω by 0.4 and 0.6 of a metre, which is not the balance condition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Two bulbs rated 60 W, 220 V and 100 W, 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply; the 60 W bulb glows brighter.
Reason (R): In a series connection the same current flows through both bulbs, so the bulb of larger resistance dissipates more power (P = I²R).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Power in series combinations
solution.explanation: From P = V²/R at the rated voltage, the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (R = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω against 484 Ω). In series the current is common, so P = I²R is larger for the 60 W bulb and it glows brighter. R is true and is exactly why A happens.
steps: Series: same I, so P ∝ R → the 60 W bulb dissipates more → A true
R states the reason: P = I²R with common current → correct explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B would need R to be unrelated to A, but R is the very reason. Many students expect the 100 W bulb to be brighter, which is true only in parallel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy and power
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Six identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are meant to be connected in series across a 5 Ω resistor, but one cell is connected the wrong way round. The current in the 5 Ω resistor is:

solution.concept: Cells in series with one reversed
solution.explanation: A reversed cell subtracts its emf, cancelling one correctly connected cell as well, so the net emf falls by 2ε. Its internal resistance still adds to the circuit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.125 A ignores the reversal (9 V across 8 Ω). 0.9375 A removes only one cell's emf (7.5 V). 1.2 A ignores the internal resistances.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about cells are correct?

(a) The emf of a cell is the potential difference between its terminals when no current is drawn from it.
(b) While a cell is being charged by an external source, its terminal voltage is greater than its emf.
(c) When n identical cells are connected in parallel, the emf of the combination is n times the emf of one cell.
(d) When two cells are connected in series, the internal resistance of the combination is the sum of their internal resistances.
(e) The emf of a cell depends on the external resistance connected across it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Emf, terminal voltage and combinations of cells
solution.explanation: Emf is a property of the cell (its electrodes and electrolyte); the terminal voltage differs from it by Ir, with the sign set by the direction of current through the cell.
steps: (a) True: on open circuit V = ε
(b) True: during charging current enters the positive terminal, V = ε + Ir
(c) False: identical cells in parallel give emf ε (only the internal resistance becomes r/n)
(d) True: r_eq = r₁ + r₂ in series
(e) False: the emf does not depend on the external circuit; the terminal voltage does
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (c) or (e) is wrong; any option leaving out (a), (b) or (d) is incomplete.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf and internal resistance; cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a conductor carrying a fixed current, doubling its cross-sectional area doubles the drift speed of its free electrons.
Statement II: For a fixed potential difference across a conductor, doubling its length halves the drift speed of its free electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Drift speed: v_d = I/(neA) and v_d = eEτ/m
solution.explanation: At fixed current, v_d = I/(neA) ∝ 1/A, so doubling A halves v_d: Statement I is false. At fixed potential difference V, the field is E = V/l, and v_d = eEτ/m = eVτ/(ml) ∝ 1/l, so doubling l halves v_d: Statement II is true.
steps: Fixed I: v_d ∝ 1/A → doubling A halves v_d → I false
Fixed V: E = V/l, v_d = eτV/(ml) ∝ 1/l → doubling l halves v_d → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I reverses the dependence on area; it would be true only for v_d ∝ A, which is not the case.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (SI unit).

List-I:
A. Resistivity
B. Conductivity
C. Mobility of charge carriers
D. Current density

List-II:
I. A m⁻²
II. Ω m
III. m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹
IV. S m⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Units from defining relations
solution.explanation: Write each quantity from its defining equation: ρ = RA/l, σ = 1/ρ, µ = v_d/E, j = I/A.
steps: Resistivity ρ = RA/l → Ω m² / m = Ω m → II
Conductivity σ = 1/ρ → Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ = S m⁻¹ → IV
Mobility µ = v_d/E → (m s⁻¹)/(V m⁻¹) = m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ → III
Current density j = I/A → A m⁻² → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The usual slip is swapping resistivity (Ω m) and conductivity (S m⁻¹), or giving mobility the unit of velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity, conductivity and mobility
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected in series with two resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω. A 4 µF capacitor is connected directly across the 3 Ω resistor. In the steady state, the charge on the capacitor is:

solution.concept: Capacitor in a DC circuit in steady state
solution.explanation: Once the capacitor is fully charged no current flows through its branch, so the circuit current is set by the resistors alone. The capacitor then has the same potential difference as the resistor it is connected across.
steps: Steady state: no current through the capacitor branch
V across 3 Ω = 2 × 3 = 6 V = V across the capacitor
solution.why_others_wrong: 28.8 µC ignores the internal resistance (I = 2.4 A, V = 7.2 V). 48 µC puts the full emf across the capacitor. 16 µC uses the voltage across the 2 Ω resistor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a metre bridge experiment, the known resistance is chosen so that the null point lies near the middle of the wire.
Reason (R): The balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge is P/Q = R/S, which does not involve the resistance of the galvanometer.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Metre bridge practice and Wheatstone bridge balance
solution.explanation: A is true: a null point near the middle keeps the two lengths comparable, so the end resistances (at the copper strips) and the error in reading l have the least effect on the result. R is also true: at balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so its resistance does not appear. But R does not explain why the null point should be near the middle; that is about reducing percentage error and end error.
steps: A true: null point near 50 cm minimises percentage error and end effects
R true: balance P/Q = R/S is independent of the galvanometer resistance
R is a property of balance, not the reason for choosing a mid-wire null point → option B
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A is the trap: both statements are correct facts about the bridge, but the galvanometer's resistance has nothing to do with where the null point should lie.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A carbon resistor (temperature coefficient of resistance −5 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹) and a metal wire resistor (temperature coefficient +5 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹) are connected in series. Their total resistance is 11 Ω and does not change, to first order, when the temperature changes slightly. The resistance of the carbon resistor is:

solution.concept: Combining positive and negative temperature coefficients
solution.explanation: In series the changes in resistance add: ΔR = (R_c α_c + R_m α_m) ΔT. For no net change this bracket must be zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 Ω is the metal resistor, obtained by swapping the coefficients. 5.5 Ω splits the total equally, which would need equal and opposite coefficients. 0.1 Ω inverts the ratio of the coefficients and drops the total.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twelve identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are to be arranged in a mixed grouping (equal rows in parallel, each row having the same number of cells in series) to send the largest possible current through an external resistance of 3 Ω. The largest current obtainable is:

solution.concept: Mixed grouping of cells: maximum current when the total internal resistance equals R
solution.explanation: With n cells in series in each of m rows (nm = 12), I = nε/(R + nr/m). The current is largest when nr/m = R.
steps: Condition: n/m = 3 and nm = 12 → n = 6, m = 2
Total emf = 6 × 2 = 12 V; internal resistance = 6 × 1/2 = 3 Ω
Check: all 12 in series gives 24/15 = 1.6 A; all in parallel gives 2/(3 + 1/12) ≈ 0.65 A
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 A is all cells in series. 0.65 A is all cells in parallel. 4 A takes 12 V across 3 Ω and forgets the internal resistance of the grouping.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the temperature dependence of resistivity are correct?

(a) In a metal, resistivity increases with temperature mainly because the average time between collisions of the electrons decreases.
(b) The resistivity of an intrinsic semiconductor decreases as its temperature rises.
(c) Alloys such as manganin and constantan are used in standard resistors because their resistivity changes very little with temperature.
(d) Every conductor obeys Ohm's law at all temperatures.
(e) The number density of free electrons in a metal increases greatly with temperature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Why resistivity changes with temperature: ρ = m/(ne²τ)
solution.explanation: In metals n is nearly fixed and τ falls with temperature, so ρ rises. In semiconductors n rises sharply with temperature and outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ falls. Manganin and constantan have very weak temperature dependence. Ohm's law is not universal (diodes, semiconductors, materials with non-linear V–I graphs).
steps: (a) True: τ decreases as ions vibrate more
(c) True: used in wire-bound standard resistors
(e) False: in a metal n does not change appreciably with temperature
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) take the semiconductor reason and apply it to metals; options with (d) treat Ohm's law as a universal law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity; limitations of Ohm's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A circular loop lies flat on a horizontal table. Seen from above, a steady current flows anticlockwise in it. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is directed:

options.text: horizontally, in the plane of the loop
vertically upwards, out of the table

solution.concept: Direction of the field of a circular loop: right-hand thumb rule
solution.explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the current; the thumb gives the field at the centre. For an anticlockwise current seen from above, the thumb points up, towards the observer.
steps: Every element of the loop gives dB at the centre along the same axis (Biot-Savart: dl × r̂)
Anticlockwise current seen from above → field along the upward normal
solution.why_others_wrong: Downwards is the result for a clockwise current. The field at the centre is along the axis, not in the plane of the loop, and contributions of all elements add, so it is not zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop
solution.final_answer: Option C: vertically upwards, out of the table

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a steady current of 10 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance of 5 cm from the wire is:

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire from Ampere's circuital law: B = µ₀I/(2πr)
solution.explanation: Take a circle of radius r around the wire as the Amperian loop. By symmetry B is constant on it and tangential, so B(2πr) = µ₀I.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁵ T uses 4πr in the denominator. 8 × 10⁻⁵ T drops the 2. 4 × 10⁻⁷ T leaves r in centimetres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (SI unit).

List-I:
A. Magnetic dipole moment
B. Magnetic field (B)
C. Magnetic flux
D. Permeability of free space (µ₀)

List-II:
I. Wb (T m²)
II. T m A⁻¹
III. A m²
IV. N A⁻¹ m⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Units of magnetic quantities
solution.explanation: Use defining relations: m = IA, F = ILB (so B = F/(IL)), Φ = BA and B = µ₀I/(2πr).
steps: Magnetic moment m = IA → A m² → III
B = F/(IL) → N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (= tesla) → IV
Φ = BA → T m² = weber → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The common mix-ups are B with flux (T against T m²) and magnetic moment with flux.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Which one of the following substances is diamagnetic?

solution.concept: Classification of magnetic materials
solution.explanation: Diamagnetic substances have a small negative susceptibility and are weakly repelled by a magnet. Bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water and sodium chloride are examples.
steps: Aluminium and sodium: paramagnetic (χ small, positive)
solution.why_others_wrong: Aluminium and sodium are paramagnetic; iron is ferromagnetic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A square coil of side 10 cm has 20 turns and carries a current of 2 A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T with the plane of the coil parallel to the field. The torque on the coil is:

solution.concept: Torque on a current loop: τ = NIAB sin θ, θ measured between the area vector and B
solution.explanation: When the plane of the coil is parallel to B, its area vector (normal) is perpendicular to B, so θ = 90° and the torque is maximum.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero takes θ as the angle between the plane and B; θ is measured from the normal. 0.4 N m is the magnetic moment, not the torque. 2.0 N m takes the area as 0.1 m².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long parallel straight wires 4 cm apart carry currents of 5 A and 8 A in the same direction. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the force per unit length between the wires is:

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents: F/L = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
solution.explanation: Each wire sits in the field of the other. Currents in the same direction attract; opposite currents repel.
solution.why_others_wrong: Repulsive is the case for opposite currents. 1 × 10⁻⁴ N/m uses 4πd; 4 × 10⁻⁴ N/m drops the 2 in 2πd.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', force between two parallel currents

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton and an alpha particle, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference and then enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles to it. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's circular path to that of the proton (r_α : r_p) is:

solution.concept: Radius of a charged particle in a magnetic field: r = mv/(qB) = √(2mK)/(qB)
solution.explanation: After acceleration through V, K = qV, so the momentum is √(2mqV) and r = √(2mV/q)/B ∝ √(m/q).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 is the ratio of m/q without the square root. 1 : 1 assumes equal momenta. 1 : √2 inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 10 mA. To convert it into an ammeter of range 0–1 A, one should connect:

solution.concept: Conversion of a galvanometer into an ammeter: low shunt in parallel
solution.explanation: At full scale, I_g flows through the galvanometer and the rest, I − I_g, through the shunt. Both have the same potential difference.
steps: The shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.99 Ω divides by I instead of (I − I_g). A series resistor converts the galvanometer into a voltmeter, not an ammeter. 11 Ω takes I_g as 100 mA instead of 10 mA.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 40 Ω shows full-scale deflection for a current of 5 mA. To use it as a voltmeter of range 0–10 V, the resistance required and its connection are:

solution.concept: Conversion of a galvanometer into a voltmeter: high resistance in series
solution.explanation: At full scale, the whole 10 V appears across the galvanometer and the series resistance, with current I_g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2000 Ω is the total resistance of the voltmeter, not the added resistance. 2040 Ω adds G instead of subtracting it. A parallel resistor would make an ammeter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a fixed current and a fixed number of turns per unit length, the magnetic field inside a long solenoid increases with the radius of the solenoid.
Statement II: Inside a long straight cylindrical wire carrying a steady current spread uniformly over its cross-section, the magnetic field increases linearly with distance from the axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Applications of Ampere's circuital law
solution.explanation: For a long solenoid, Ampere's law with a rectangular loop gives B = µ₀nI, which has no dependence on the radius: Statement I is false. Inside a uniform wire of radius a, a circular loop of radius r < a encloses current I r²/a², so B(2πr) = µ₀I r²/a² and B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²) ∝ r: Statement II is true.
steps: Solenoid: B = µ₀nI, independent of radius → I false
Inside the wire: I_enc = I r²/a² → B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²) ∝ r → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses the solenoid with a single loop, whose central field does depend on radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law; the solenoid
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about a bar magnet are correct?

(a) The magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet is similar to that of a current-carrying solenoid of the same shape.
(b) The potential energy of a bar magnet in a uniform magnetic field is minimum when its magnetic moment is parallel to the field.
(c) A bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences no net force.
(d) At equal large distances, the field of a short bar magnet at an axial point is half the field at an equatorial point.
(e) The torque on a bar magnet in a uniform field is maximum when its magnetic moment is parallel to the field.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: The bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid; dipole in a uniform field
solution.explanation: A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid with the same magnetic moment. In a uniform field the forces on its two ends cancel (no net force) but there is a torque τ = mB sin θ, and its energy is U = −mB cos θ.
steps: (a) True: NCERT compares the bar magnet with an equivalent solenoid
(b) True: U = −mB cos θ is least (−mB) at θ = 0°
(c) True: equal and opposite forces on the poles in a uniform field
(d) False: B_axial = 2µ₀m/(4πr³) is twice B_equatorial = µ₀m/(4πr³)
(e) False: τ = mB sin θ is zero at θ = 0° and maximum at 90°
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) has the axial and equatorial fields the wrong way round. (e) confuses the position of minimum energy with that of maximum torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet; magnetic dipole in a uniform field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (type of material) with List-II (magnetic susceptibility χ).

List-I:
A. Diamagnetic material
B. Paramagnetic material
C. Ferromagnetic material
D. Superconductor (perfect diamagnet)

List-II:
I. χ = −1
II. small and positive
III. large and positive (χ ≫ 1)
IV. small and negative

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Susceptibility of magnetic materials
solution.explanation: χ measures how strongly a material is magnetised by a field. It is small and negative for diamagnets, small and positive for paramagnets, very large and positive for ferromagnets, and exactly −1 for a superconductor, which expels the field completely (Meissner effect).
steps: Diamagnetic: −1 < χ < 0, small in magnitude → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Taking a superconductor as merely 'small and negative' misses that it expels the field completely.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long wire is bent into a hairpin shape: two long straight parallel portions joined by a semicircle of radius R. A current I flows through it. The magnetic field at the centre of the semicircle is:

solution.concept: Biot-Savart law: semicircular arc plus semi-infinite straight wires
solution.explanation: The centre of the semicircle lies on the line through the ends of the two straight portions. Each straight portion is a semi-infinite wire ending at the foot of the perpendicular from the centre, and all three parts give fields in the same direction at the centre.
steps: Each semi-infinite wire: B = (µ₀I/4πR)(sin 90° + sin 0°) = µ₀I/(4πR)
Two wires: µ₀I/(2πR) = (µ₀I/4R)(2/π), same direction as B₁
solution.why_others_wrong: µ₀I/4R ignores the straight portions. (1 + 1/π) counts only one straight wire. (1 − 2/π) takes the straight portions as opposing the arc; but the two wires lie on opposite sides of the centre and carry opposite currents, so both fields point the same way as the arc's.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field with a velocity that makes an angle of 60° with the direction of the field. It moves along a helix. The ratio of the pitch of the helix to its radius is:

solution.concept: Helical motion: components of velocity along and across B
solution.explanation: The component v sin θ perpendicular to B gives circular motion of radius r = mv sin θ/(qB) and period T = 2πm/(qB). The component v cos θ along B carries the particle forward a distance p = (v cos θ)T in each turn.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2π√3 uses tan θ instead of cot θ (components swapped). π/√3 uses half a period. √3/(2π) is the ratio r/p.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Protons pass undeflected through a region with a uniform electric field of 3 × 10⁴ V/m and a uniform magnetic field of 0.02 T, perpendicular to each other and to the protons' velocity. The electric field is now switched off. Taking the proton mass as 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and its charge as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the radius of the circular path of the protons in the magnetic field is:

solution.concept: Velocity selector followed by circular motion in B
solution.explanation: Undeflected motion means qE = qvB, which fixes the speed. With E removed, the magnetic force alone provides the centripetal force.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 m takes B as 0.01 T in the last step. 0.375 m brings in a spurious factor of 1/2. 1.33 m is the inverse, qB/(mv).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Increasing the number of turns of a moving-coil galvanometer always increases its voltage sensitivity.
Reason (R): The current sensitivity of a moving-coil galvanometer is NAB/k, where k is the torsional constant of the spring.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Current and voltage sensitivity of a moving-coil galvanometer
solution.explanation: Current sensitivity φ/I = NAB/k, so R is true. Voltage sensitivity φ/V = NAB/(kR_G). If N is doubled using the same kind of wire, the length of wire and hence R_G also double, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same. A is false.
steps: At equilibrium NIAB = kφ → φ/I = NAB/k → R true
φ/V = NAB/(kR_G); doubling N doubles R_G → φ/V unchanged → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: Increasing N raises current sensitivity, not necessarily voltage sensitivity; options A, B and C all accept A, which ignores the coil's resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet form continuous closed loops.
(b) The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.
(c) Two magnetic field lines can intersect at a point where the field is strong.
(d) The susceptibility of a paramagnetic material decreases as its temperature rises.
(e) A diamagnetic substance placed in a non-uniform magnetic field moves from the weaker towards the stronger region of the field.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Field lines, Gauss's law for magnetism and magnetic materials
solution.explanation: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end, so as many lines leave a closed surface as enter it. Lines cannot cross, because the field has one direction at each point. Paramagnetic susceptibility follows Curie's law, χ ∝ 1/T. Diamagnets are pushed from stronger to weaker field regions.
steps: (a) True: lines are closed loops (continue inside the magnet)
(b) True: Gauss's law for magnetism, Φ_B = 0 for any closed surface
(c) False: two lines crossing would mean two directions of B at one point
(e) False: a diamagnet moves from the stronger to the weaker region
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) describes a paramagnet, not a diamagnet. (c) is never true for field lines.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetism and Gauss's law; magnetic properties of materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The magnetic flux through each turn of a 200-turn coil decreases uniformly from 5 mWb to 1 mWb in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the average emf induced in the coil is:

solution.concept: Faraday's law: |ε| = N |ΔΦ|/Δt
solution.explanation: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage, NΦ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.04 V leaves out the 200 turns. 12 V adds the initial and final fluxes. 2 V uses only the final flux.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alternating voltage is given by v = 311 sin(100πt) volt, with t in seconds. The rms voltage and the frequency of the supply are approximately:

solution.concept: rms value and frequency of a sinusoidal voltage
solution.explanation: Compare with v = V₀ sin ωt: V₀ = 311 V and ω = 100π rad/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 311 V is the peak value. 100 Hz takes ω/π instead of ω/2π. 156 V divides the peak by 2 instead of √2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The SI unit of inductance, the henry (H), is equivalent to:

solution.concept: Definition of inductance: Φ = LI (flux linkage per unit current)
solution.explanation: Since NΦ = LI, L = NΦ/I, so 1 H = 1 Wb/A. Equivalently, from ε = L dI/dt, 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹.
steps: Check with ε = L dI/dt: H = V/(A s⁻¹) = V s A⁻¹ (not V A⁻¹ s⁻¹)
solution.why_others_wrong: Wb A and T m² A multiply by the current instead of dividing. V A⁻¹ s⁻¹ has the second in the wrong place.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal transformer has 500 turns in the primary and 2500 turns in the secondary. The primary is connected to a 220 V AC supply and draws a current of 5 A. The secondary voltage and secondary current are:

solution.concept: Ideal transformer: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p and V_p I_p = V_s I_s
solution.explanation: The voltage is stepped up in the ratio of turns; with no losses, power in = power out, so the current is stepped down by the same ratio.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 A steps the current up along with the voltage, which would make output power 25 times the input. 44 V uses the turns ratio upside down.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod of length 0.5 m slides on two parallel frictionless rails with a speed of 4 m/s, perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T (the field is perpendicular to the plane of the rails). The rails are connected through a 2 Ω resistor; all other resistance is negligible. The external force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed is:

solution.concept: Motional emf and the magnetic force on the induced current
solution.explanation: The moving rod has emf Blv, which drives a current through the resistor. The field exerts a force BIl on this current that opposes the motion (Lenz's law); at constant speed the applied force must balance it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.25 N uses l instead of l² in B²l²v/R. 0.0625 N divides by 4 Ω instead of 2 Ω. 1.0 N is the emf in volts read as a force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.2 H increases from 2 A to 4 A. The increase in the magnetic energy stored in the coil is:

solution.concept: Energy stored in an inductor: U = ½LI²
solution.explanation: The stored energy depends on the square of the current, so the change must be found as a difference of squares, not from the change in current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.4 J uses (ΔI)² instead of the difference of the squares. 2.4 J drops the ½. 1.6 J is the final energy, not the increase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit has L = 0.5 H, C = 2 µF and R = 40 Ω, and is connected to an AC source of rms voltage 200 V whose frequency can be varied. The resonant angular frequency and the rms current at resonance are:

solution.concept: Series resonance: ω₀ = 1/√(LC), Z = R
solution.explanation: At resonance X_L = X_C, so the reactances cancel and the impedance is the resistance alone.
steps: At resonance Z = R = 40 Ω, so I_rms = 200/40 = 5 A
solution.why_others_wrong: 159 is the resonant frequency in hertz (ω₀/2π), not in rad/s. 3.5 A divides the rms current by √2 again. 500 rad/s has a spurious factor of ½.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Lenz's law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy.
Statement II: The mutual inductance of two coils depends on the currents flowing in them.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Lenz's law and mutual inductance
solution.explanation: If the induced current aided the change that produced it, the change would grow by itself and energy would be created; so Lenz's law follows from energy conservation (Statement I true). Mutual inductance depends only on the geometry of the coils (number of turns, size, separation, orientation) and the permeability of the medium, not on the currents (Statement II false).
steps: Statement I: true (opposition to change is required by energy conservation)
Statement II: false (M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l for coaxial solenoids: geometry and medium only)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II mixes up M with the flux linkage MI, which does depend on current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy; mutual inductance
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I with List-II for a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source of angular frequency ω.

List-I:
A. Inductive reactance
B. Capacitive reactance
C. Resonant angular frequency
D. Impedance at resonance

List-II:
I. 1/√(LC)
II. R
III. ωL
IV. 1/(ωC)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reactance, impedance and resonance
solution.explanation: X_L = ωL and X_C = 1/(ωC). Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); at resonance X_L = X_C, which gives ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and Z = R.
steps: Resonant angular frequency: ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C) → ω₀ = 1/√(LC) → I
Impedance at resonance: Z = R → II
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping X_L and X_C is the usual slip: an inductor's opposition grows with frequency, a capacitor's falls.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; resonance
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series circuit contains a 30 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 80 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω, connected to a 200 V (rms) AC supply. The average power consumed in the circuit is:

solution.concept: Power in an AC circuit: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = I_rms² R
solution.explanation: Only the resistor consumes power on average; the inductor and capacitor store and return energy each cycle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 800 W is the apparent power V_rms I_rms, ignoring the power factor. 1333 W is V²/R, taking the full supply voltage across the resistor. 640 W uses the net reactance (40 Ω) in place of R.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small coil of 200 turns and radius 1 cm is placed coaxially well inside a long solenoid that has 1000 turns per metre. The current in the long solenoid is increased at a steady rate of 50 A/s. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the emf induced in the small coil is about:

solution.concept: Mutual inductance of coaxial coils: M = µ₀ n N π r²
solution.explanation: The long solenoid's field µ₀nI is uniform inside it, so the flux linkage of the small coil is N(µ₀nI)(πr²), where r is the radius of the small coil.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.8 mV takes the diameter (2 cm) as the radius. 0.395 mV takes 100 turns per metre. 1.26 mV leaves out the π in the area πr².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A strong magnet dropped into a long vertical copper tube falls with an acceleration less than g.
Reason (R): The current induced in the walls of the tube exerts a force on the magnet that aids its fall.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Lenz's law applied to a falling magnet
solution.explanation: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the tube changes, inducing currents in the copper (copper itself is not attracted by the magnet). By Lenz's law these currents oppose the cause, i.e. the relative motion, so they exert an upward force on the magnet. A is true; R is false because the force opposes the fall.
steps: Changing flux through rings of the tube → induced currents
Lenz's law: induced effect opposes the motion → upward force on the magnet
Net downward force < mg → acceleration < g: A true; R false
solution.why_others_wrong: A force that aided the fall would increase the magnet's kinetic energy without any source of energy, which Lenz's law (energy conservation) forbids.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about transformers are correct?

(a) A transformer works on the principle of mutual induction.
(b) In an ideal step-up transformer, the current in the secondary coil is smaller than the current in the primary coil.
(c) A transformer can be used to step up a steady DC voltage.
(d) The core of a transformer is laminated to reduce energy loss due to eddy currents.
(e) In an ideal step-up transformer, the output power is greater than the input power.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Working and energy losses of a transformer
solution.explanation: An alternating current in the primary produces a changing flux that links the secondary (mutual induction). A steady DC gives no changing flux, so nothing is induced. In an ideal transformer V_pI_p = V_sI_s, so stepping voltage up steps current down and the power stays the same.
steps: (b) True: V_s > V_p with V_pI_p = V_sI_s → I_s < I_p
(c) False: constant flux induces no emf
(d) True: laminations reduce eddy currents in the core
(e) False: power out = power in for an ideal transformer
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) would violate energy conservation; (c) ignores that induction needs a changing flux.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (part of the electromagnetic spectrum) with List-II (a use).

List-I:
A. Microwaves
B. Infrared
C. Ultraviolet
D. X-rays

List-II:
I. Detecting fractures in bones
II. Killing germs in water purifiers
III. Radar systems used in aircraft navigation
IV. Lamps used in physical therapy

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Uses of different parts of the EM spectrum
solution.explanation: Each band is used where its interaction with matter is useful: microwaves for radar, infrared for heating (physical therapy), ultraviolet to kill germs, and X-rays because they pass through soft tissue but not bone.
steps: Microwaves → radar for aircraft navigation → III
Infrared → infrared lamps in physical therapy → IV
Ultraviolet → UV lamps kill germs in water purifiers → II
X-rays → medical diagnosis, e.g. fractures → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The likely slip is swapping infrared (heating) and ultraviolet (germicidal).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance 2 µF is being charged so that the potential difference between its plates increases at a rate of 5 × 10⁴ V/s. The displacement current in the region between the plates is:

solution.concept: Displacement current: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt
solution.explanation: Between the plates no charge flows, but the electric flux changes. For a parallel-plate capacitor ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀A dE/dt = (ε₀A/d) dV/dt = C dV/dt, which equals the conduction current in the leads.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero ignores Maxwell's displacement current. 2.5 × 10¹⁰ A divides dV/dt by C. 0.05 A brings in a spurious factor of ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In vacuum, electromagnetic waves of higher frequency travel faster than those of lower frequency.
Statement II: In an electromagnetic wave, the oscillating electric and magnetic fields are parallel to each other.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Nature of electromagnetic waves
solution.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum with the same speed c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀), whatever their frequency, so Statement I is false. E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, so Statement II is false.
steps: Statement I: speed in vacuum = c for all frequencies → false
Statement II: E ⊥ B ⊥ direction of propagation → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Dispersion (speed depending on frequency) happens in a material medium, not in vacuum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum along the +x direction. At a certain point and instant its electric field is 6 V/m along the +y direction. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the magnetic field at that point and instant is:

solution.concept: Relation between E and B in an EM wave: B = E/c, with E × B along the direction of propagation
solution.explanation: In an EM wave E and B are in phase, so B = E/c at every point and instant. The direction of E × B gives the direction of propagation, which fixes the direction of B.
steps: E along +y, propagation along +x: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so B is along +z
solution.why_others_wrong: −z would make E × B point along −x. 1.8 × 10⁹ T multiplies by c instead of dividing. B cannot be along x, the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image is formed:

options.text: 10 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror

solution.concept: Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian sign convention)
solution.explanation: With distances measured from the pole and negative in front of the mirror: u = −30 cm and f = −15 cm. The object is at the centre of curvature, so the image is also at the centre of curvature.
steps: v = −30 cm → real image 30 cm in front of the mirror
m = −v/u = −1: inverted and of the same size
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 cm comes from writing 1/v = 1/f + 1/u (the lens-type sign slip). 'Behind the mirror' would be a virtual image, which a concave mirror forms only for objects inside the focus.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 30 cm in front of the mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens of focal length 25 cm is placed in contact with a thin concave lens of focal length 50 cm. The power of the combination is:

solution.concept: Power of thin lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂, with P = 1/f (f in metres)
solution.explanation: A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens negative power; powers of lenses in contact add.
solution.why_others_wrong: +6 D treats the concave lens as converging. −2 D gets the sign of the result wrong. +0.02 D uses focal lengths in centimetres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A cut diamond sparkles brilliantly because light entering it undergoes multiple total internal reflections before coming out.
Reason (R): The critical angle for the diamond–air interface is very small (about 24.4°).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Total internal reflection in diamond
solution.explanation: Diamond has a large refractive index (about 2.42), so its critical angle is small, about 24.4°. Light that enters a suitably cut diamond strikes the inner faces at angles larger than this and is totally reflected many times, coming out only from a few directions. The small critical angle is the reason for the multiple reflections, so R explains A.
steps: Most rays inside meet faces at more than 24.4° → repeated TIR
Both true, and R is the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate fact here: without the small critical angle there would be no multiple total internal reflection.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following phenomena shows that light waves are transverse?

solution.concept: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves
solution.explanation: Only a transverse wave has a direction of vibration perpendicular to its direction of travel that can be selected (polarised). Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
steps: Interference and diffraction occur for all waves, transverse or longitudinal
Reflection occurs for waves and particles alike
Polarisation needs vibrations perpendicular to the direction of propagation → transverse
solution.why_others_wrong: Interference and diffraction prove wave nature, not the transverse character.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A prism of angle 60° produces an angle of minimum deviation of 30°. The refractive index of the material of the prism is:

solution.concept: Prism formula at minimum deviation: n = sin[(A + δm)/2]/sin(A/2)
solution.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, with r = A/2 and i = (A + δm)/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: √3 uses sin 60°/sin 30° (forgets to add δm and halve). 1/√2 inverts the ratio. 1.5 is only a typical value for glass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (instrument and adjustment) with List-II (magnifying power). Here f, f_o and f_e are focal lengths, L is the tube length and D is the least distance of distinct vision.

List-I:
A. Simple microscope, final image at the near point
B. Simple microscope, final image at infinity
C. Astronomical telescope in normal adjustment
D. Compound microscope, final image at infinity

List-II:
I. f_o/f_e
II. (L/f_o)(D/f_e)
III. D/f
IV. 1 + D/f

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Magnifying power of optical instruments
solution.explanation: A simple microscope gives 1 + D/f with the image at the near point and D/f with the image at infinity. A telescope in normal adjustment gives f_o/f_e. A compound microscope with the final image at infinity gives m_o × m_e = (L/f_o)(D/f_e).
steps: Simple microscope, near point: m = 1 + D/f → IV
Simple microscope, infinity: m = D/f → III
Telescope, normal adjustment: m = f_o/f_e → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The usual slip is swapping the two simple-microscope cases: the extra '1 +' appears only when the image is at the near point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A tank contains a 20 cm deep layer of water (refractive index 4/3) with a 12 cm thick layer of oil (refractive index 1.5) floating on it. Viewed from directly above, the bottom of the tank appears to be at a depth below the top surface of the oil of:

solution.concept: Apparent depth for near-normal viewing: each layer contributes (real thickness)/n
solution.explanation: For viewing along the normal, a layer of thickness t and refractive index n appears to have thickness t/n. The apparent depths of successive layers add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 cm treats both layers as water. 21.3 cm treats both as oil. 9 cm is the apparent shift (32 − 23), not the apparent depth.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin biconvex lens of glass (refractive index 1.5) has both radii of curvature equal to 20 cm. When it is completely immersed in water (refractive index 4/3), its focal length becomes:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with a surrounding medium: 1/f = (n_lens/n_medium − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: Bending at each surface depends on the refractive index of the glass relative to the medium around it. In water this relative index is much closer to 1, so the lens becomes much weaker.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm is the focal length in air. 26.7 cm multiplies the air value by 4/3. 40 cm doubles it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 0.5 mm apart, the screen is 1 m away and light of wavelength 600 nm (in air) is used. If the entire apparatus is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3, the fringe width becomes:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d, with the wavelength in the medium
solution.explanation: In water the frequency is unchanged but the wavelength falls to λ/n, so the fringe width falls by the same factor.
steps: In water: λ' = λ/n, so β' = β/n
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 mm is the fringe width in air. 1.6 mm multiplies by n instead of dividing. 0.6 mm halves the air value.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.1 mm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 2 m away. The linear width of the central maximum is:

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction: first minima at a sin θ = ±λ
solution.explanation: The central maximum extends between the first minima on either side, at angles ±λ/a for small angles.
steps: Distance of first minimum from centre = Dθ = 2 × 5 × 10⁻³ = 1 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 cm is the distance from the centre to the first minimum (half-width). 4 cm doubles again. 0.5 cm uses the half-width with D = 1 m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction at a single slit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two polaroids whose pass axes are inclined at 60° to each other. The intensity of the light coming out of the second polaroid is:

solution.concept: Malus' law: I = I₁ cos² θ
solution.explanation: The first polaroid passes half the intensity of unpolarised light, whatever its orientation. The second follows Malus' law with θ = 60°.
steps: After the first polaroid: I₁ = I₀/2
After the second: I₂ = (I₀/2) cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8
solution.why_others_wrong: I₀/4 applies cos² 60° to I₀ directly, forgetting the first halving. 3I₀/8 uses sin² 60°. I₀/2 stops after the first polaroid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When light is incident on a transparent medium at Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other.
Statement II: When unpolarised light is incident at Brewster's angle, the refracted light is completely plane polarised.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Polarisation by reflection: Brewster's law, tan i_B = n
solution.explanation: At Brewster's angle the reflected ray is completely polarised and is perpendicular to the refracted ray (i_B + r = 90°), so Statement I is true. The refracted light is only partially polarised, because it still contains most of both components; Statement II is false.
steps: tan i_B = n with Snell's law gives sin r = cos i_B → r + i_B = 90° → I true
Only the reflected light is fully polarised; the transmitted light is partially polarised → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II attributes to the refracted beam what is true only of the reflected beam.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation by reflection
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Young's double-slit experiment performed with white light, the central fringe is coloured.
Statement II: Two independent sodium lamps cannot act as coherent sources, because the phase difference between the light from them changes rapidly and randomly with time.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Interference with white light; coherent sources
solution.explanation: At the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours interfere constructively and the central fringe is white (Statement I false). Light from independent sources has a phase difference that changes randomly in about 10⁻¹⁰ s, so the pattern averages out; they are incoherent (Statement II true).
steps: Path difference zero at centre for all λ → bright for all colours → white → I false
Independent sources: random phase changes → incoherent → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: The fringes on either side of the centre are coloured, which is where the idea of a coloured central fringe comes from.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves; interference
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (observation) with List-II (phenomenon mainly responsible).

List-I:
A. Light guided along a bent optical fibre
B. Bright and dark fringes in Young's double-slit experiment
C. Light spreading into the geometrical shadow behind a narrow slit
D. Polaroid sunglasses cutting down glare

List-II:
I. Diffraction
II. Polarisation
III. Total internal reflection
IV. Interference

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Identifying wave-optics and ray-optics phenomena
solution.explanation: Optical fibres trap light by repeated total internal reflection; Young's fringes come from superposition of two coherent waves; bending into the shadow is diffraction; polaroids block one plane of vibration.
steps: Optical fibre → total internal reflection → III
Spreading behind a slit → diffraction → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Interference and diffraction are often swapped: two coherent sources give interference; bending at one narrow opening is diffraction.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A convex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 converges light whatever medium it is placed in.
Reason (R): The focal length of a lens depends on the refractive index of its material relative to the surrounding medium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with a surrounding medium
solution.explanation: By the lens maker's formula, 1/f = (n_lens/n_medium − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂), so R is true. If the medium is optically denser than the glass (for example carbon disulphide, n ≈ 1.63), n_lens/n_medium < 1, f becomes negative and the biconvex lens diverges light. So A is false.
steps: In a medium with n > 1.5: (n_lens/n_medium − 1) < 0 → f < 0 → diverging → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is true only when the surrounding medium is optically rarer than the glass, as with air or water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens: lens maker's formula
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object and a screen are fixed 100 cm apart. A convex lens placed between them forms a sharp image on the screen at two positions of the lens that are 20 cm apart. The focal length of the lens is:

solution.concept: Displacement method: f = (D² − d²)/(4D)
solution.explanation: By the reversibility of light, the two positions are symmetric: in one, the object distance equals the image distance of the other. So u + v = D and v − u = d.
steps: u + v = 100 and v − u = 20 → u = 40 cm, v = 60 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 cm is D/4, the largest focal length for which an image can be formed at all. 26 cm adds d² instead of subtracting it. 20 cm takes the displacement itself as f.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. An object is placed 1.25 cm in front of the objective, and the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm. The magnitude of the magnifying power of the microscope is:

solution.concept: Compound microscope: m = m_o × m_e, with m_e = 1 + D/f_e for the final image at the near point
solution.explanation: The objective forms a real, magnified image; the eyepiece acts as a simple microscope on this image.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 uses m_e = D/f_e, which is for the final image at infinity. 30 takes m_o as v/f_o = 5. 6 is the eyepiece magnification alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light falls normally on one face of a prism of angle 30° made of glass of refractive index √2. The angle through which the ray is deviated by the prism is:

solution.concept: Refraction through a prism: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A
solution.explanation: At normal incidence the ray enters undeviated (i = r₁ = 0), so it meets the second face at r₂ = A = 30°.
steps: At the second face: sin e = n sin r₂ = √2 × ½ = 1/√2 → e = 45°
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° is the angle of emergence, not the deviation. 12.4° uses the thin-prism formula δ = (n − 1)A, which is not valid for a 30° prism at normal incidence. 30° is the prism angle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the intensities of light from the two slits at the screen are in the ratio 4 : 9. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern is:

solution.concept: Interference of waves of unequal amplitude: I_max ∝ (a₁ + a₂)², I_min ∝ (a₁ − a₂)²
solution.explanation: Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so first convert the intensity ratio to an amplitude ratio.
solution.why_others_wrong: 169 : 25 adds and subtracts the intensities instead of the amplitudes. 9 : 4 is just the ratio of the source intensities. 5 : 1 forgets to square the amplitude sums.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the refraction of light are correct?

(a) When light passes from a denser to a rarer medium, the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence.
(b) When light passes from air into glass, its wavelength decreases.
(c) When light passes from air into glass, its frequency decreases.
(d) Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from air into water.
(e) The speed of light in glass is less than its speed in air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Refraction: Snell's law and what changes at a boundary
solution.explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction. In a denser medium the speed falls (v = c/n), so the wavelength λ = v/f falls too. Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium.
steps: (a) True: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r with n₁ > n₂ gives r > i
(d) False: TIR needs denser → rarer; air → water is rarer → denser
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) is the classic trap: the colour (frequency) of light does not change on entering glass. (d) reverses the condition for total internal reflection.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction; total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about diffraction at a single slit and about polaroids are correct?

(a) The intensity of the secondary maxima decreases as their order increases.
(b) The first minimum of the pattern occurs at an angle θ given by a sin θ = λ/2, where a is the slit width.
(c) The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
(d) Increasing the width of the slit makes the central maximum wider.
(e) Polaroids can be used to control the intensity of light, for example in sunglasses and window panes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction pattern; uses of polaroids
solution.explanation: The first minima are at a sin θ = ±λ, so the central maximum has angular width 2λ/a, twice that of the secondary maxima, and it narrows when the slit is widened. Secondary maxima get progressively weaker. A polaroid transmits only one plane of vibration, so turning it controls the transmitted intensity.
steps: (a) True: secondary maxima fade with order
(b) False: first minimum at a sin θ = λ
(c) True: central width 2λ/a vs λ/a for the others
(e) True: polaroids in sunglasses, window panes and photographic filters
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) uses the condition for a path difference of half a wavelength between the edges, which is not a minimum. (d) inverts the dependence on slit width.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction at a single slit; polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The energy of a photon of wavelength 620 nm is (take hc = 1240 eV nm):

solution.concept: Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ
solution.explanation: With hc expressed in eV nm, dividing by the wavelength in nm gives the energy directly in eV.
steps: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm / 620 nm = 2 eV
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 eV inverts the formula (λ/hc). 20 eV and 0.2 eV are slips of a factor of 10 in the division.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Using λ = 1.227/√V nm, its de Broglie wavelength is about:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts
solution.explanation: The electron gains kinetic energy eV, so p = √(2meV) and λ = h/p = h/√(2meV) = 1.227/√V nm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.227 nm forgets to divide by √V. 0.0123 nm divides by V instead of √V. 12.27 nm multiplies by √V.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the incident light is increased while its frequency (above the threshold) is kept the same. Which of the following increases?

options.text: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
The threshold frequency of the metal

solution.concept: Effect of intensity on photoelectric emission
solution.explanation: Greater intensity at a fixed frequency means more photons per second, so more electrons are emitted per second and the saturation current rises. Each photon still has the same energy hν, so the maximum kinetic energy and the stopping potential do not change.
steps: Number of photons per second ∝ intensity → saturation current ∝ intensity
K_max = hν − φ₀: unchanged at fixed ν → stopping potential unchanged
Threshold frequency depends only on the metal
solution.why_others_wrong: Maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential depend on frequency, not intensity. The threshold frequency is a property of the metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of intensity of light on photocurrent
solution.final_answer: Option B: The saturation photoelectric current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal surface whose work function is 2.0 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the stopping potential is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: eV₀ = hν − φ₀
solution.explanation: The stopping potential is the reverse potential that just stops the fastest photoelectrons, so eV₀ = K_max.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 V uses the photon energy without subtracting the work function. 6 V adds the work function. 1 V halves K_max.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is the same for all metals.
Statement II: The stopping potential depends on the work function of the metal but not on the frequency of the incident light.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Threshold frequency and stopping potential
solution.explanation: The threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h depends on the work function, which differs from metal to metal, so Statement I is false. From eV₀ = hν − φ₀, the stopping potential depends on both the frequency of light and the work function, so Statement II is false.
steps: ν₀ = φ₀/h, different for different metals → I false
V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e: increases linearly with ν → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is half right: V₀ does depend on φ₀, but it also rises with frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of frequency of incident radiation on stopping potential
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A proton and an alpha particle, both initially at rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle (λ_p : λ_α) is:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength after acceleration: λ = h/√(2mqV)
solution.explanation: Through the same V, each particle gains K = qV, so the momentum is √(2mqV) and λ ∝ 1/√(mq).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 is the answer for equal kinetic energies (charge ignored). √2 : 1 uses only the charge ratio. 1 : 2√2 inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Photoelectric emission begins practically instantaneously (within about 10⁻⁹ s) after light falls on the metal, even when the light is very dim.
Reason (R): The energy of a photon is proportional to the intensity of the light.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Photon picture of the photoelectric effect
solution.explanation: A is an experimental fact explained by the photon picture: a single photon gives all its energy hν to a single electron at once, so there is no time needed to accumulate energy. R is false: a photon's energy is hν and depends only on frequency; the intensity decides how many photons arrive per second.
steps: A true: no observable time lag, even at low intensity
R false: E = hν, independent of intensity
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B accept R, which mixes up photon energy with photon number.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect; Einstein's photoelectric equation
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: When a metal surface is illuminated with light of wavelength λ, the stopping potential is 3.0 V. When it is illuminated with light of wavelength 2λ, the stopping potential is 0.5 V. The work function of the metal is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation for two wavelengths
solution.explanation: Write eV₀ = hc/λ − φ₀ for both cases; doubling the wavelength halves the photon energy. Two equations give both the photon energy and the work function.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 eV is the photon energy at 2λ, 5.0 eV the photon energy at λ, and 0.5 eV the second stopping potential; none of them is the work function.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A laser emits light of wavelength 660 nm with a power of 3 mW. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the number of photons it emits per second is:

solution.concept: Photon flux: N = P/(hc/λ)
solution.explanation: The beam's power is the energy carried per second, and each photon carries hc/λ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10¹⁹ takes 3 mW as 3 W. 1 × 10¹³ takes it as 3 µW. 3 × 10¹⁶ takes the photon energy as 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, dropping the factor 3 from c.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases linearly with the frequency of the incident light.
(b) The slope of the graph of stopping potential against frequency is h/e, the same for all metals.
(c) Below the threshold frequency, photoelectrons are emitted if the light is intense enough.
(d) A proton and an electron that have the same de Broglie wavelength have the same momentum.
(e) The de Broglie wavelength of a particle does not depend on its speed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Photoelectric equation and de Broglie relation
solution.explanation: K_max = hν − φ₀ is a straight line in ν (not a proportionality), and eV₀ = hν − φ₀ gives a slope h/e for every metal. Below ν₀ no electron gets enough energy from one photon, however many photons arrive. λ = h/p, so equal λ means equal momentum, and λ changes with speed.
steps: (c) False: no emission below ν₀ at any intensity
(d) True: λ = h/p → same λ, same p
(e) False: λ = h/(mv) falls as speed rises
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) is the classical-wave expectation that the photoelectric effect disproves. (e) ignores p = mv.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation; wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, the energy of the hydrogen atom in its nth state is −13.6/n² eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from a hydrogen atom in its first excited state is:

solution.concept: Energy levels of hydrogen; ionisation from an excited state
solution.explanation: The first excited state is n = 2. Removing the electron means taking it to n = ∞, where its energy is zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state. 10.2 eV is the excitation energy from n = 1 to n = 2. 6.8 eV divides 13.6 by n instead of n².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The radius of a nucleus of mass number A is R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ = 1.2 fm. The radius of a nucleus with A = 125 is:

solution.concept: Size of the nucleus: R = R₀A^(1/3)
solution.explanation: Nuclear volume is proportional to A, so the radius grows as the cube root of A.
