solution.why_others_wrong: 150 fm multiplies by A itself. 13.4 fm uses the square root of A. 0.24 fm divides R₀ by 5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, most of the alpha particles passed through the gold foil without any appreciable deflection. This observation shows that:

options.text: the positive charge of an atom is spread uniformly over the atom
electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits
most of the space inside an atom is empty

solution.concept: Conclusions from alpha-particle scattering
solution.explanation: If the alpha particles meet nothing massive or highly charged on most paths, the atom must be mostly empty space. The rare large-angle deflections showed that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
steps: Most particles undeflected → most of the atom is empty space
A few deflected by large angles → tiny, massive, positively charged nucleus
solution.why_others_wrong: A uniform spread of positive charge (Thomson's model) cannot produce the rare large-angle scattering. The experiment says nothing about electron orbits or neutrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle scattering and Rutherford's nuclear model of atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: most of the space inside an atom is empty

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mass defect of a certain nucleus is 0.02 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², its binding energy is:

solution.concept: Mass–energy equivalence: E_b = Δm c²
solution.explanation: The binding energy is the energy equivalent of the mass defect.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.863 MeV and 186.3 MeV misplace the decimal point. 9.315 MeV halves the result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The ratio of the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series to that of the first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen is:

solution.concept: Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
solution.explanation: The first line of a series is the transition from the next higher level: 2 → 1 for Lyman and 3 → 2 for Balmer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 : 5 is the inverse ratio (energies, not wavelengths). 3 : 4 and 4 : 9 compare only parts of the two brackets.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is 0.53 Å. The radius of the orbit with n = 3 in a singly ionised helium ion (He⁺, Z = 2) is:

solution.concept: Bohr radius for hydrogen-like ions: r_n = 0.53 n²/Z Å
solution.explanation: The radius grows as n² and shrinks as 1/Z because the larger nuclear charge pulls the electron closer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.77 Å ignores Z. 1.59 Å uses n instead of n² and ignores Z. 0.795 Å uses n/Z instead of n²/Z.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom are correct?

(a) The lines of the Lyman series lie in the ultraviolet region.
(b) In a stationary orbit, the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2π.
(c) The total energy of the electron in the nth orbit is −13.6/n² eV.
(d) The speed of the electron in its orbit increases as n increases.
(e) An electron in a stationary orbit radiates energy continuously.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bohr's postulates and their consequences
solution.explanation: Bohr postulated that the electron moves in certain stationary orbits without radiating, with L = nh/2π. It radiates only when it jumps between orbits. In these orbits r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n and E = −13.6/n² eV. Transitions to n = 1 (Lyman series) have the largest energies and lie in the ultraviolet.
steps: (a) True: Lyman series in the ultraviolet
(d) False: v_n ∝ 1/n, so speed falls as n rises
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) is what classical physics predicts and Bohr's postulate denies. (d) reverses v ∝ 1/n.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom; the line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The density of nuclear matter is nearly the same for all nuclei.
Statement II: The nuclear force between two nucleons is nearly independent of their charge and acts only over very short distances, of the order of a few femtometres.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Nuclear density and the nuclear force
solution.explanation: Since R = R₀A^(1/3), the nuclear volume is proportional to A and so is the mass; the density is therefore nearly the same (about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei. The nuclear force is short-ranged and nearly the same for n–n, n–p and p–p pairs.
steps: Volume ∝ R³ ∝ A and mass ∝ A → density independent of A → I true
Nuclear force: short range, charge independent → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are standard NCERT facts; neither is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus; nuclear force
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I:
A. Nuclear fission
B. Nuclear fusion
C. Mass defect
D. Maximum binding energy per nucleon

List-II:
I. Nuclei near A = 56 (iron)
II. Main source of the Sun's energy
III. Basis of the energy produced in a nuclear reactor
IV. Difference between the total mass of the free nucleons and the mass of the nucleus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Fission, fusion and binding energy
solution.explanation: Reactors use controlled fission of heavy nuclei. The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium. The mass defect is the mass that disappears when nucleons bind. Binding energy per nucleon peaks (about 8.75 MeV) near A = 56.
steps: Fusion → energy of the Sun → II
Mass defect → Σ(nucleon masses) − nuclear mass → IV
Peak of B/A curve → A ≈ 56 → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping fission and fusion is the usual slip: reactors use fission; stars use fusion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass–energy and nuclear binding energy; nuclear energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nucleus of mass number 240, with a binding energy of 7.6 MeV per nucleon, splits into two nuclei of mass number 120 each, with a binding energy of 8.5 MeV per nucleon. The energy released in the process is:

solution.concept: Energy released = (total binding energy of products) − (total binding energy of the parent)
solution.explanation: Energy is released because the products are more tightly bound; the gain in binding energy appears as kinetic energy of the fragments.
solution.shortcut: Total nucleon number is unchanged, so Q = 240 × (8.5 − 7.6) = 216 MeV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 108 MeV counts only one fragment. 0.9 MeV is the gain per nucleon. 432 MeV counts the gain twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alpha particle with a kinetic energy of 5 MeV is directed head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Taking e²/(4πε₀) = 1.44 MeV fm, the distance of closest approach is about:

solution.concept: Distance of closest approach: K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d
solution.explanation: In a head-on approach the alpha particle stops momentarily when all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy (the heavy gold nucleus is taken as fixed).
solution.why_others_wrong: 22.8 fm takes the alpha particle's charge as e instead of 2e. 91.0 fm doubles once more. 4.55 fm is a decimal slip.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle trajectory; distance of closest approach

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Photons emitted when hydrogen atoms make the transition from n = 4 to n = 2 fall on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Taking E_n = −13.6/n² eV, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is:

solution.concept: Hydrogen spectrum combined with Einstein's photoelectric equation
solution.explanation: The photon energy equals the difference of the two energy levels. Subtract the work function to get K_max.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.55 eV forgets the work function. 10.75 eV uses the 4 → 1 transition (12.75 eV). 0.85 eV is the magnitude of the n = 4 energy, not a transition energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Energy is released both in the fusion of very light nuclei and in the fission of very heavy nuclei.
Reason (R): The binding energy per nucleon is smaller for very light nuclei and for very heavy nuclei than for nuclei of intermediate mass number.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Binding energy curve and nuclear energy
solution.explanation: B/A is low for light nuclei, rises to about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238 (this is R, which is true). Fusing light nuclei or splitting a heavy nucleus gives products with higher B/A, that is, more tightly bound, and the extra binding energy is released (A, true). So R explains A.
steps: R true: shape of the B/A versus A curve
A true: fusion and fission both move towards higher B/A
Higher B/A of the products is why energy is released → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B is the trap: R is not merely related; the binding energy curve is exactly why both processes release energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass–energy and nuclear binding energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following impurities, when added in small amounts to pure silicon, makes it a p-type semiconductor?

solution.concept: Extrinsic semiconductors: acceptor (trivalent) impurities
solution.explanation: A trivalent atom such as boron, aluminium or indium has only three valence electrons, so one bond with neighbouring silicon atoms is incomplete. This creates a hole, making holes the majority carriers.
steps: Trivalent dopant (B, Al, Ga, In) → acceptor → p-type
Pentavalent dopant (As, P, Sb) → donor → n-type
solution.why_others_wrong: Arsenic, phosphorus and antimony are pentavalent donors, which make n-type silicon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A full-wave rectifier is supplied with a 50 Hz AC input. The fundamental frequency of the ripple in its output is:

solution.concept: Output of a full-wave rectifier
solution.explanation: A full-wave rectifier sends current through the load in the same direction in both halves of each input cycle, so the output has two pulses per input cycle.
steps: Output: 2 pulses per input cycle → 100 pulses per second → 100 Hz
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 Hz is the ripple frequency of a half-wave rectifier. 25 Hz halves instead of doubling. 200 Hz doubles twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A two-input logic gate gives an output 0 only when both its inputs are 1, and an output 1 for every other combination of inputs. The gate is:

solution.concept: Truth tables of basic logic gates
solution.explanation: Y = 0 only for A = B = 1 is the opposite of AND (which gives 1 only for A = B = 1). This is the NAND gate, Y = (A·B)'.
steps: AND: Y = 1 only when A = B = 1
NAND = NOT(AND): Y = 0 only when A = B = 1
NOR: Y = 1 only when A = B = 0; OR: Y = 0 only when A = B = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: AND has the opposite outputs. NOR gives 1 only for both inputs 0. OR gives 0 only for both inputs 0.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A silicon crystal has an intrinsic carrier concentration of 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³. It is doped so that the electron concentration becomes 4.5 × 10²² m⁻³. In thermal equilibrium, the hole concentration is:

solution.concept: Mass-action law: n_e n_h = n_i²
solution.explanation: Doping raises one carrier concentration and, by recombination, lowers the other, keeping the product equal to n_i².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ is the intrinsic value, which applies only before doping. 4.5 × 10²² m⁻³ assumes equal numbers of holes and electrons. 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ m⁻³ divides n_i by n_e without squaring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode with a breakdown voltage of 6 V is used as a voltage regulator. It is connected through a 200 Ω series resistor to a 10 V DC supply, and a 1 kΩ load resistor is connected across the Zener diode. The current through the Zener diode is:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: current division between Zener and load
solution.explanation: In breakdown the Zener holds 6 V across itself and the load. The series resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage and carries the total current, which splits between the load and the Zener.
steps: Voltage across series resistor = 10 − 6 = 4 V → I_s = 4/200 = 20 mA
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 mA is the current in the series resistor. 6 mA is the load current. 26 mA adds the load current instead of subtracting it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Inputs A and B are each passed through a NOT gate, and the two outputs are fed to an AND gate. The circuit as a whole behaves as:

solution.concept: Combining gates; De Morgan's theorem
solution.explanation: The output is Y = A'·B'. By De Morgan's theorem A'·B' = (A + B)', which is the NOR function.
steps: Output 1 only for both inputs 0 → NOR
solution.why_others_wrong: NAND would be A' + B' (inverted inputs into an OR gate). OR and AND have different truth tables.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a p-n junction is forward biased, the width of its depletion region decreases.
Statement II: The small current in a reverse-biased p-n junction diode is due to the majority charge carriers.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Biasing of a p-n junction
solution.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, lowering the barrier and narrowing the depletion region (Statement I true). In reverse bias the barrier rises, majority carriers cannot cross, and the small current (of the order of µA) is due to minority carriers drifting across the junction (Statement II false).
steps: Forward bias: barrier height and depletion width decrease → I true
Reverse current: drift of minority carriers → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Majority carriers produce the large forward current, not the small reverse current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction under forward and reverse bias
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A photodiode is operated under reverse bias.
Reason (R): Under reverse bias, the fractional change in current caused by light is much larger than the fractional change under forward bias.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why a photodiode is reverse biased
solution.explanation: Light creates electron–hole pairs that add to the minority-carrier current. Under forward bias this extra current is tiny compared with the large majority-carrier current, so it is hard to detect. Under reverse bias the dark current is very small, so the same photocurrent is a large fraction of it. This is precisely why photodiodes are reverse biased.
steps: A true: photodiodes are used in reverse bias
R true: minority-carrier current is small, so light changes it by a large fraction
R is the reason for A → option A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B would require R to be unrelated to A, but R is the very reason given in NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices: photodiode
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (device) with List-II (how it is operated or used).

List-I:
A. Light emitting diode
B. Photodiode
C. Solar cell
D. Zener diode in a voltage regulator

List-II:
I. Reverse biased, used to detect optical signals
II. Operated in the reverse breakdown region
III. Forward biased, emits light
IV. No external bias; generates an emf when light falls on it

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Special-purpose p-n junction devices
solution.explanation: An LED emits light when electrons and holes recombine under forward bias. A photodiode is reverse biased to detect light. A solar cell needs no bias; light generates an emf. A Zener diode regulates voltage in its reverse breakdown region.
steps: LED → forward biased, emits light → III
Photodiode → reverse biased, detects light → I
Solar cell → no external bias, generates emf → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping the photodiode and the solar cell is the usual slip: one is a detector that needs reverse bias, the other a source of emf with no bias.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', special purpose p-n junction diodes
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected in series with a 1 kΩ resistor to two parallel branches. Branch P contains an ideal diode that is forward biased by the battery, in series with a 2 kΩ resistor. Branch Q contains an ideal diode that is reverse biased by the battery, in series with a 1 kΩ resistor. The current drawn from the battery is:

solution.concept: Ideal diodes in DC circuits
solution.explanation: An ideal diode is a short circuit when forward biased and an open circuit when reverse biased. So branch Q carries no current and the circuit reduces to 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series.
steps: Branch Q: reverse-biased diode → open → no current
Branch P: forward-biased diode → short → 2 kΩ
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.6 mA lets both branches conduct (2 kΩ ∥ 1 kΩ in series with 1 kΩ). 3 mA lets only branch Q conduct. 1.5 mA adds all three resistors in series.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An LED has a forward voltage of 2.0 V when it carries its rated current of 20 mA. It is to be run from a 9 V DC supply through a series resistor. The resistance needed and the power dissipated in that resistor are:

solution.concept: Series resistor for an LED: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I
solution.explanation: The LED fixes its own forward voltage; the resistor must drop the remaining voltage at the rated current.
steps: Power in resistor = I²R = (0.02)² × 350 = 0.14 W (= 7 V × 0.02 A)
solution.why_others_wrong: 450 Ω and 0.18 W ignore the LED's forward voltage. 0.04 W is the power in the LED (2 V × 20 mA), not in the resistor. 100 Ω uses the LED's voltage instead of the resistor's.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about semiconductors are correct?

(a) In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number density of free electrons equals that of holes.
(b) In a p-type semiconductor, holes are the minority carriers.
(c) Doping silicon with a trivalent impurity produces an n-type semiconductor.
(d) The energy band gap of silicon is larger than that of germanium.
(e) In an n-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority carriers, and the material as a whole is electrically neutral.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
solution.explanation: In a pure crystal each thermally freed electron leaves one hole, so n_e = n_h. Trivalent dopants give holes (p-type), with holes as the majority carriers; pentavalent dopants give electrons (n-type). Doping adds neutral atoms, so a doped crystal stays neutral. The band gap is about 1.1 eV for Si and 0.7 eV for Ge.
steps: (b) False: holes are the majority carriers in p-type
(e) True: majority electrons, but overall neutral
solution.why_others_wrong: A common misconception is that n-type material is negatively charged; it is neutral, because every donor electron leaves behind a positive donor ion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about rectifiers and the Zener diode are correct?

(a) In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier, both diodes conduct at the same time.
(b) The output of a rectifier without a filter is a pulsating (fluctuating) DC voltage.
(c) A Zener diode is made by heavily doping both its p- and n-sides, which makes its depletion region very thin.
(d) In a half-wave rectifier, current flows through the load during only one half of each input cycle.
(e) A Zener voltage regulator keeps the output voltage nearly constant even when the input voltage changes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rectifier action and Zener regulation
solution.explanation: In a centre-tap rectifier the two diodes conduct in alternate half-cycles. Without a filter, the output is unidirectional but pulsating. A Zener diode is heavily doped, so its depletion layer is thin and the field is strong enough for breakdown at a low, sharp voltage; in breakdown the voltage across it stays nearly constant over a wide range of current.
steps: (c) True: heavy doping, thin depletion layer
(d) True: half-wave rectifier passes one half-cycle
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) are wrong; the option with only (b), (d) and (e) leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', rectifier; Zener diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a vernier calipers, one main scale division is 1 mm and 10 vernier scale divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions. While measuring the diameter of a rod (with no zero error), the main scale reading is 2.4 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides with a main scale division. The diameter of the rod is:

solution.concept: Vernier calipers: least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD; reading = MSR + (VSC × LC)
solution.explanation: The least count is the difference between one main-scale and one vernier-scale division.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.406 cm takes the least count as 0.01 mm. 3.00 cm adds 6 mm instead of 6 × 0.1 mm. 2.94 cm adds 6 × 0.9 mm, the length of 6 vernier divisions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (laboratory set-up) with List-II (quantity it is used to determine).

List-I:
A. Metre bridge
B. Resonance tube
C. Steel ball falling at terminal velocity through glycerine
D. Capillary rise in a glass tube

List-II:
I. Surface tension of water
II. Speed of sound in air
III. Resistivity of the material of a wire
IV. Coefficient of viscosity of the liquid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Standard NEET laboratory experiments
solution.explanation: Each set-up isolates one quantity: a metre bridge compares resistances, a resonance tube finds λ at a known frequency, terminal velocity in a viscous liquid gives η by Stokes' law, and capillary rise gives surface tension.
steps: Metre bridge → unknown resistance → resistivity ρ = RA/l → III
Resonance tube → resonating lengths → λ → v = fλ → II
Capillary rise h → S = hρgr/(2 cos θ) → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Mixing up the two fluid experiments (viscosity and surface tension) is the most likely slip.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. With the studs closed it shows a positive zero error of +0.03 mm. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the main scale reading is 3.5 mm and the 42nd circular division is on the reference line. The corrected diameter of the wire is:

solution.concept: Screw gauge: least count = pitch/number of circular divisions; true reading = observed reading − zero error
solution.explanation: A positive zero error means the gauge reads too much, so it is subtracted from every reading.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.95 mm adds the positive zero error instead of subtracting it. 3.92 mm ignores the zero error. 3.68 mm takes the least count as 0.005 mm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the simple pendulum experiment, the time for 20 or more oscillations is measured rather than the time for a single oscillation.
Reason (R): Timing many oscillations reduces the least count of the stop-watch.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Reducing percentage error in timing
solution.explanation: The least count of a stop-watch is fixed by its design (for example 0.1 s) and the reaction-time error at start and stop is about the same however long the timing is. Spreading this fixed error over 20 periods makes the error in one period, and the percentage error, 20 times smaller. So A is true and R is false.
steps: A true: standard practice for the pendulum experiment
R false: the least count does not change; the percentage error in T falls
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B accept R; the least count is a property of the instrument, not of the measurement.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the u–v method for finding the focal length of a concave mirror, a graph of 1/v against 1/u (magnitudes) is a straight line that cuts both axes at 1/f.
Statement II: In the experiment to plot the i–δ curve of a prism, the angle of deviation first decreases and then increases as the angle of incidence is increased.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Graphical methods in optics experiments
solution.explanation: For a real image formed by a concave mirror, 1/|v| + 1/|u| = 1/|f|, a straight line of slope −1 with both intercepts equal to 1/|f| (Statement I true). For a prism, δ falls to a minimum (δm) at one angle of incidence and rises again on either side (Statement II true).
steps: 1/|v| = −1/|u| + 1/|f| → straight line, intercepts 1/f on both axes → I true
i–δ curve: δ decreases, reaches δm, then increases → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither statement is false; a graph of v against u would be a hyperbola, which is perhaps why the first statement looks doubtful.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment to find the resistivity of the material of a wire using ρ = πd²R/(4L), the percentage errors in measuring the diameter d, resistance R and length L are 1%, 2% and 0.5% respectively. The maximum percentage error in ρ is:

solution.concept: Propagation of errors: for ρ = k dᵃ Rᵇ L⁻ᶜ, Δρ/ρ = a(Δd/d) + b(ΔR/R) + c(ΔL/L)
solution.explanation: Relative errors add for products and quotients, each multiplied by the power of the quantity. Errors are always added, even for quantities in the denominator.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.5% forgets the power 2 on d. 2.5% leaves out d altogether. 5.0% counts the error in L twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment, a steel ball of diameter 2 mm (density 7800 kg/m³) falls through glycerine (density 1050 kg/m³) and reaches a terminal velocity of 5 cm/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the coefficient of viscosity of glycerine is:

solution.concept: Stokes' law at terminal velocity: v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η)
solution.explanation: At terminal velocity the weight is balanced by buoyancy plus viscous drag, 6πηrv_t = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.15 Pa s drops the factor 2. 1.2 Pa s uses the diameter as the radius. 0.35 Pa s ignores buoyancy (uses ρ instead of ρ − σ).
